UNNAMED FOLDER

Fourteen photos. The first is from 2014: the Larchmont, in flames, and him with his back to the fire, looking at the neighbor's camera. The last is from 2025: Harbor Island, under a streetlight.

Same face. Same scar, from the right cheekbone to the lip. Same coat, or one just like it. Same way of standing: feet apart, weight back, like the ground's about to move.

Eleven years and not one gray hair.

He shows up in four of my cases. Always after. Never during. He arrives when the worst is over and leaves before the police get there. Once I watched him clean a scene like someone sweeping a kitchen.

He gave me a phone. He said my name without my telling him.

I don't know what he is. I don't know if he's good. I know he's looking out for me, and I don't know why.

Follow-up: find out who died in 1960 with his face.

2017 · BELLEVUE PARKING GARAGE

A fifty-year-old man jumps from the fifth floor of an office parking garage. He'd lost everything on a takeover bid that went bad that same afternoon. Suicide. Case closed.

But there's a still from the third-floor security camera, at 11:47 p.m. A young woman, dark hair, expensive coat, crouched beside him before he jumps. She's touching his face. He doesn't look scared. He looks calm.

Four minutes later, he jumps. She's gone.

I looked her up. She works in finance. In one of the photos from a 2019 gala, she looks the same as in 2017. Exactly the same. Same haircut.

I don't think she pushed him. I think she was there for something else. I don't know what.

Follow-up: why does someone go looking for people who've just lost everything?

2018 · PIONEER SQUARE

A thermal camera at a light rail construction site recorded this on March 8 at 3:12 a.m.: a human figure lifts a manhole cover and climbs down. In the thermal image, everything around it has color. The figure doesn't. It's dark blue, like the water in the Sound. Like something that's been dead a while.

The figure turned up on the same camera six more times that year. Always in the small hours. Always the same manhole.

And one more thing, which I don't know is connected: in the last video, before climbing down, the figure looks toward the camera. And the camera shuts off. Eleven minutes.

Exactly like the ones in my building the night of the break-in.

Follow-up: who shuts off the cameras in this city?

SEVERAL YEARS · N.

This is strange to write.

N. has produced my podcast since 2021. She's the best producer I've ever had. She sends me leads and I don't know where she gets them. They always come in at three in the morning.

Going through event photos for something else, I noticed: she isn't in a single group photo. Not one. At the episode 100 party, the whole team is in the picture and she isn't. She was there. I remember she was there. I remember she hugged me.

I asked her once and she said she hates photos. Could be.

I don't like having opened this folder. I opened it anyway. It's what I do.

Follow-up: none. I don't want a follow-up on her.

2023 · THE RUNNING MAN

A cell phone video, Ballard, July 14, 2023, 1:40 a.m. A car tears out of a parking lot. A big man, blond, beard, fisherman's jacket, runs after it.

And he catches it.

Not in some long chase. In about a hundred yards. The car's doing forty. The man pulls up alongside, opens the driver's door while it's moving, and the video cuts out because whoever's filming drops the phone.

The next day there's no police report, no accident, nothing. The car turned up at the harbor, parked and clean.

I have another photo of that man in a fishermen's bar from 1998. Clipped from a local paper. Same.

Follow-up: the Ballard bars. Someone has to know him.

2021 · THE IMPOSSIBLE REPORTS

Fifteen autopsy reports from the county M.E.'s office between 2008 and 2021. I got them one at a time, with favors and with patience. Every one has something strange: a body with “severe unexplained hypovolemia,” a fire that didn't burn what it should have, an “animal bite” with a pattern no animal leaves.

And every one has the same calm conclusion, the same reasonable explanation. Overdose. Accident. Animal.

And the same signature: R. A., night-shift pathologist.

I don't think she's crazy. I think she's very good at her job. What I don't know is who she works for.

Follow-up: ask her for an interview. No. Not yet.

Format: One sheet per PC. Delivery: Session zero or @UUID[JournalEntry.5hwXPdn0tUJ3NaKZ.JournalEntryPage.T8gJWjZpOnL4OisP]{A1-E01 · What They Took}.

Storyteller: one sheet per character. It's what Helen had on each of them, written in her voice, like her working notes. Hand it out privately. If a player creates their own character, write theirs in this same style based on what they decide in session zero.

David's (@UUID[JournalEntry.3zcQLj7aEAxHT0Yr]{David Smith}) isn't handed to anyone: David is an NPC. It's the folder Helen kept on him, the “unnamed folder” with the fourteen photos. The coterie can read it in the “SAFE” folder on USB drive 3 (@UUID[JournalEntry.FttkHsYSSaCpIugu.JournalEntryPage.5Vgl8slqjXlVRbie]{A2-E06 · The One Who Kept One}). Whether they show it to David, and what they tell him about what Helen wrote, is up to the players.
